papers.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26920v1

summary.one_liner: Across 12 LLMs from six families, the native coordinate axes of hidden representations align better with other models, with human brain responses, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes do, though they fall short of the best achievable alignment ("partially canonical").
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether the individual numbered directions inside a large language model's internal state mean anything, or whether only combinations of them carry meaning. They compared each model's native axes with versions of the same data rotated to random orientations. The native axes matched other models, human brain activity during language, and simple linguistic features somewhat better than the rotated ones, but not as well as the best possible alignment.
summary.why: It challenges the common assumption that individual units in language models are arbitrary, which matters for interpretability work that inspects single neurons. The link to human brain responses is suggestive, but the text alone does not show how strong or useful that link is for theory.
summary.background:
- Hidden representation: the vector of numbers a model holds internally for a word or sentence.
- Coordinate axis: one of the individual numbered dimensions of that vector, the "neuron" or unit.
- Rotation: changing the orientation of the whole space, which preserves distances and overall geometry but scrambles which axis is which.
- Alignment: how closely two sets of representations match in structure, often measured by how well one predicts the other.
- Canonical vs arbitrary: "canonical" here means the axes pick out special, meaningful directions; "arbitrary" means any rotation would do equally well.
- Brain responses: recordings of human brain activity while people read or hear language, used as a comparison target.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

papers.title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27211v1

summary.one_liner: SP-Refine makes style extraction an explicit inference-time step for personalized long-form generation, using a 28-aspect taxonomy (StylePrism) to build a user style profile that guides drafting and two rounds of self-revision on LongLaMP tasks.
summary.plain: Language models asked to write in a specific person's voice usually just receive a few of that person's past texts and have to guess what matters about their style. This paper proposes a fixed checklist of 28 style features in seven groups, has the model fill that checklist in from the user's writing, and then drafts and revises text against it. On three long-form writing tasks with three models, the method beat the standard retrieval-based baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average.
summary.why: Personalizing AI writing to individuals is a practical goal, and making style explicit rather than implicit may make it easier to inspect and control. The reported gains are measured on automatic overlap metrics only, and the ablations suggest the profile works best as revision guidance alongside the user's samples, so the benefit beyond these tasks is unclear.
summary.background:
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): putting relevant example texts into a model's prompt before it writes.
- Long-form generation: producing multi-paragraph text such as articles or reviews, not short answers.
- ROUGE and METEOR: automatic scores that measure word overlap between generated text and a reference text.
- Inference-time method: a technique applied when the model is run, without retraining it.
- Ablation: a test that removes one part of a method to see how much it contributes.
- Oracle variant: a version that peeks at the answer, used to estimate an upper bound on gains.

papers.abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.
